# KindTech

# Home

## Home

# KindTech

Ergonomic Python access to UK public data. Geographic boundaries from the ONS ArcGIS Geoportal, statistics from the NOMIS API — with universal DataFrame support.

## Try it now — no install

Run a real notebook in your browser. Each one fetches live ONS data through the molab cloud runtime:

<div class="grid cards" markdown>

-   __ONS statistics__

    ---

    Browse and load datasets straight from the NOMIS API.

    [![Open in molab](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/ons_statistics.py)

-   __Geographic boundaries__

    ---

    Explore LAD, LSOA and other UK boundary data interactively.

    [![Open in molab](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/geo_boundaries.py)

-   __Boundaries + statistics__

    ---

    Join geographic shapes with ONS data and map the result.

    [![Open in molab](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/geo_plus_ons.py)

</div>

## Install

Install [uk-open-data from PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/uk-open-data/):

```bash
uv add uk-open-data
```

KindTech depends on requests, narwhals, and python-calamine. You bring your own
DataFrame library (pandas or polars). The [package FAQ](faq/README.md) explains
which subpackages are included and how they are released.

## Quick start

```python
from uk_open_data import load_geodata, load_ons, geodata_to_properties
import pandas as pd  # or polars

# Load LAD boundaries (GeoJSON) and extract properties
geojson = load_geodata(geography_type="LAD", year="2024")
geo_df = pd.DataFrame(geodata_to_properties(geojson, "LAD", 2024))

# Load ONS statistics — columns are normalised automatically
ons_df = load_ons("population", geography_type="LAD", time="latest")

# Join on the shared geography_code column
merged = geo_df.merge(ons_df, on="geography_code")
```

## Bring Your Own DataFrame

KindTech uses [narwhals](https://narwhals-dev.github.io/narwhals/) for universal DataFrame support. The library itself has **no pandas or polars dependency** — it returns whatever backend you have installed.

```python
# With pandas installed → returns pd.DataFrame
from uk_open_data.ons import load_ons
df = load_ons("NM_1_1")
type(df)  # <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'>
```

```python
# With polars installed → returns pl.DataFrame
from uk_open_data.ons import load_ons
df = load_ons("NM_1_1")
type(df)  # <class 'polars.dataframe.frame.DataFrame'>
```

If both are installed, polars is preferred (it's faster and more memory-efficient). The geo module returns plain GeoJSON dicts — no DataFrame backend needed.

## Why does this exist?

UK public data is powerful but painful to access programmatically. The ONS ArcGIS Geoportal has no developer documentation — just a point-and-click GUI. The REST API endpoint was discovered buried in the source code of an obscure UK government R package. NOMIS is slightly better documented but requires deep knowledge of SDMX query syntax and dataset codes that aren't surfaced anywhere obvious.

Every charity, social enterprise, and researcher working with UK geographic or statistical data ends up reverse-engineering the same APIs independently. KindTech wraps them so you don't have to — two function calls instead of hours of documentation archaeology.

## Modules

- [**Geographic Data**](api/geo.md) — UK boundary data from ArcGIS (LAD, LSOA, etc.)
- [**ONS Statistics**](api/ons.md) — 1,615 datasets from the NOMIS API
- [**Case Studies**](case-studies/index.md) — Real-world examples from the charity sector

# Case Studies

## Overview

# Case Studies

End-to-end reproductions of real [DataKind UK](https://www.datakind.org.uk/)
charity projects, rebuilt with KindTech. Each one chains several connectors on a
shared `geography_code`, and — because real client data is private — pairs the
public data with a transparent synthetic stand-in so the full analysis runs.

Every study has a runnable [marimo](https://marimo.io/) notebook: open it in the
molab cloud runtime to run it **in your browser** (it fetches live ONS data), or
locally with `uv run marimo edit examples/<notebook>.py`.

| Case study | What it shows | Run |
|---|---|---|
| [Smart Works](smart-works-woman-unemployment.md) | Women's unemployment vs service reach (Census 2021 + LAD boundaries) | [![Open in molab](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/smart_works_unemployment.py) |
| [Citizens Advice Lewisham](cal-vulnerable-client.md) | Deprivation vs service usage (postcodes + IMD + LSOA boundaries) | [![Open in molab](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/cal_vulnerable_client.py) |
| [Sobus](sobus-bame-analysis.md) | BAME mental-health referrals in Hammersmith & Fulham (outcodes + Census ethnicity) | [![Open in molab](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/sobus_bame_referrals.py) |
| [Starlight](starlight-children-mapping.md) | Hospital play provision vs need across ICBs | [![Open in molab](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/starlight_play_provision.py) |
| [Material Focus](material-focus-recycling.md) | Travel time to the nearest recycling point (LAD boundaries + population) | [![Open in molab](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/material_focus_recycling.py) |

## How each study is structured

- **Problem statement** — the question the charity set out to answer.
- **Dataset involved** — the open (and, where relevant, synthetic) data used.
- **Desired output** — what the original analysis produced.
- **Reproduction with KindTech** — the connector pipeline, with figures.
- **Lessons learned** — takeaways and where the approach generalises.

## Have a case study to share?

Using KindTech in your own work? We'd love to feature it — open an issue or PR
on the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/KindTechUK/uk-open-data).


## CAL Vulnerable Client Analysis

# CAL Vulnerable Client Analysis

**Reference article:** [DataKind UK - Citizens Advice Lewisham](https://www.datakind.org.uk/stories-news/citizens-advice-lewisham)

**More about what Citizens Advice Lewisham is doing:** [Citizens Advice Lewisham](https://citizensadvicelewisham.org.uk/)

## Problem Statement

Citizens Advice Lewisham (CAL) needed to identify 'vulnerability hotspots' - areas with high need but limited access to resources - to optimize service delivery.

**Key objectives:**

- Map vulnerability hotspots in Lewisham
- Optimize service delivery based on geographic need
- Validate service targeting effectiveness

## Dataset Involved

**CAL Vulnerability Framework**: Internal assessment of service users' ability to cope with life changes, based on factors like low income, housing, mental health, and disability.

**Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD)**: Government dataset measuring seven deprivation domains (income, employment, crime, etc.) mapped to Lower Layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs) - geographic units of ~1,500 people each.

## Desired Output

**Deprivation Map**: Visual representation showing LSOAs colored by deprivation level (red = least deprived, yellow = most deprived), revealing higher deprivation in southern borough areas.

**Service Usage Map**: Geographic distribution of CAL clients per capita, with color coding indicating service demand (yellow = high usage, red = low usage).

**Key Finding**: Strong correlation between deprivation levels and service usage - areas with highest deprivation scores also showed highest client volumes, validating CAL's service targeting.

![CAL map data dashboard](../images/case-studies/deprivation-vs-client-per-capita.jpg)
*Figure 1: Geographic distribution of CAL clients per capita across Lewisham LSOAs and IMD scores*

## Replicating the Output with KindTech

### Data Requirements

**Internal Dataset:**

- Individual client records with vulnerability factor scores
- Postcode data for geographic mapping
- Goal: Map postcodes to LSOAs to calculate clients per capita

**External Datasets:**

- **Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD)**: LSOA-level deprivation scores for overlay analysis
- **Census Data**: Population figures for per-capita calculations
- **LSOA Boundaries**: Geographic polygons for spatial analysis and mapping

### Analysis Workflow

1. **Data Preparation**: Convert postcodes to LSOA codes using geographic lookup
2. **Aggregation**: Calculate total clients per LSOA
3. **Normalization**: Compute clients per capita using census population data
4. **Spatial Analysis**: Overlay client density with IMD scores
5. **Visualization**: Create comparative maps showing deprivation vs. service usage

### Reproduction

A runnable, end-to-end reproduction lives in
[`examples/cal_vulnerable_client.py`](https://github.com/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/cal_vulnerable_client.py)
(a [marimo](https://marimo.io/) notebook). It chains three KindTech connectors,
all joining on the 2021 LSOA `geography_code`:

[![Open in marimo](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/cal_vulnerable_client.py)
&nbsp;— run it live in the browser (the molab cloud runtime fetches real ONS
data), or locally with `uv run marimo edit examples/cal_vulnerable_client.py`.

```python
from uk_open_data import postcodes_to_geography, load_imd, load_geodata

# 1. Client postcodes -> LSOA (the step real client data would use)
clients = postcodes_to_geography(client_postcodes, geography_type="LSOA")

# 2. Deprivation + population per LSOA (IoD 2025, on 2021 LSOAs)
imd = load_imd(nation="England")  # imd_decile, imd_score, population
```

!!! note "Everything is on 2021 LSOAs — no crosswalk"
    The postcode connector returns 2021 LSOA codes, **IMD 2025** is published on
    2021 LSOAs (and ships a population denominator), and the default LSOA
    boundaries are 2021. So deprivation, population and client geography line up
    on one `geography_code` with no vintage conversion. (The older composite
    `load_imd(year=2019)` is on 2011 LSOAs and would need a crosswalk.)

Client records are private, so the notebook generates synthetic clients per
LSOA at a rate that **rises with deprivation**, then normalises to clients per
1,000 residents.

**Hotspots vs usage** — deprivation (left) and CAL client rate (right). Shared
dark areas mean clients come from the most-deprived LSOAs:

![Reproduced CAL maps](../images/case-studies/cal-reproduced-maps.png)
*Figure 2: IMD 2025 decile (left, dark = most deprived) vs synthetic CAL clients
per 1,000 residents (right). The hotspots align.*

**Does usage track deprivation?** Each LSOA's deprivation score against its
client rate:

![Reproduced CAL scatter](../images/case-studies/cal-reproduced-scatter.png)
*Figure 3: A clear positive correlation between deprivation and clients per
capita — the direction the original study found, validating CAL's targeting.*

To run on real data, feed the real client postcodes through step 1 and
aggregate per `geography_code`; the IMD join, per-capita maths and maps are
unchanged.

## Lessons Learned

**Key takeaways and recommendations:**

- **Geographic targeting works**: The strong correlation between deprivation and service usage validates CAL's approach to targeting high-need areas
- **Data integration is crucial**: Combining internal service data with external deprivation indices provides powerful insights
- **Visualization drives action**: Clear maps help stakeholders understand and act on the findings
- **Per-capita analysis matters**: Normalizing by population reveals true service demand patterns
- **LSOA-level granularity is appropriate**: Geographic units of ~1,500 people provide sufficient detail without compromising privacy


## Material Focus Recycling

# Material Focus Recycling Analysis

**Reference article:** [DataKind UK - Material Focus Recycling](https://www.datakind.org.uk/stories-news/material-focus)

**More about what Material Focus Recycling is doing:** [Material Focus Recycling](https://www.materialfocus.org.uk/)

## Problem Statement

Material Focus needed to gather evidence to demonstrate to stakeholders what interventions would make the greatest difference in increasing electrical item recycling rates across the UK.

**Key Research Questions**:

- Where in the UK could Material Focus achieve the greatest impact if small electricals were recycled through major supermarkets?
- Do factors like proximity to collection points influence recycling rates in different areas?
- What barriers prevent individuals from recycling electrical goods?

**Objective**: To identify optimal locations for new collection points and understand the factors that influence recycling behavior, enabling Material Focus to encourage local authorities to fund additional infrastructure.

## Dataset Involved

**Internal Data**:

- Existing recycling rates for electronic goods and general recycling
- Location of current recycling points across the UK
- Travel times from residential areas to nearest recycling facilities

**External Data**:

- Population density by geographic area
- Car ownership rates
- Housing types and demographics
- Other relevant socioeconomic variables

## Desired Output

**Travel Time Visualization**: A comprehensive map showing average travel time in minutes to any recycling location across England, with travel times ranging from a maximum of 20 minutes to under six minutes.

**Key Finding**: The visualization revealed that a significant proportion of people across England have access to recycling points within 12 minutes of travel time, indicating good baseline infrastructure coverage.

**Behavioral Analysis**: Material Focus was particularly interested in understanding what factors would influence new individuals to start recycling—not just optimizing for people already engaged in recycling. The analysis examined:

- Travel distance to recycling facilities
- Population density compared to recycling participation rates
- Availability of kerbside collection services

![Recycling map](../images/case-studies/recycling-map.jpg)
*Figure 1: Average travel time in minutes to any recycling location for people living in the area, moving from a maximum of 20 minutes to under six minutes.*

## Replicating the Output with KindTech

### Analysis Workflow

1. Generate the recycling rate data at local authority level
2. Combine with LAD boundary data to create a map of the UK

Or

1. Locate the recycling points and generate average travel time to the nearest recycling point within LAD
2. Combine with LAD boundary data to create a map of the UK

### Reproduction

A runnable, end-to-end reproduction lives in
[`examples/material_focus_recycling.py`](https://github.com/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/material_focus_recycling.py)
(a [marimo](https://marimo.io/) notebook). It builds the headline travel-time
map from two KindTech connectors, joining on `geography_code`:

[![Open in marimo](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/material_focus_recycling.py)
&nbsp;— run it live in the browser (the molab cloud runtime fetches real ONS
data), or locally with `uv run marimo edit examples/material_focus_recycling.py`.

```python
from uk_open_data import load_geodata, geodata_to_properties, load_ons
import pandas as pd

# LAD boundaries carry LAT/LONG centroids
geojson = load_geodata(geography_type="LAD", year="2025", boundary_type="BUC")
geo = pd.DataFrame(geodata_to_properties(geojson, "LAD", 2025))

# Total population per LAD — so the headline is people-weighted, not area-weighted
pop = load_ons("population", geography_type="LAD", time="latest",
               measures=20100, gender=0, c_age=200)
```

The real collection-point list isn't public, so the notebook scatters 300
synthetic points *where people live* (supermarket take-back follows population)
and measures the straight-line distance from each LAD centroid to the nearest
one.

!!! warning "Straight-line distance, not road routing"
    The original mapped **road travel time**. This reproduction approximates it
    with **haversine** distance converted to minutes at an effective 40 km/h,
    capped at 20 minutes. That reproduces the *pattern* and the headline
    statistic well, but it is not a true drive-time. A faithful road travel-time
    map needs a **routing engine** (e.g. [OSRM](https://project-osrm.org/) or
    [OpenRouteService](https://openrouteservice.org/)); KindTech does not wrap
    one yet. If more case studies need real travel time, a small `uk_open_data`
    routing connector would be worth adding.

**Travel-time map** — minutes to the nearest recycling point per LAD:

![Reproduced Material Focus map](../images/case-studies/material-focus-reproduced-map.png)
*Figure 2: Approximate travel time (minutes) to the nearest recycling point.
~76% of people are within a 12-minute trip, with a long tail of harder-to-reach
rural authorities (dark) — candidates for new collection points.*

**Does proximity influence recycling?** Each LAD's travel time against a
synthetic participation rate:

![Reproduced Material Focus scatter](../images/case-studies/material-focus-reproduced-scatter.png)
*Figure 3: A real-but-loose downward trend — recycling falls as travel time
rises, the direction Material Focus argued, with proximity one driver among
several (car ownership, kerbside collection, demographics).*

To run on real data, swap the synthetic points for Material Focus's actual
collection-point coordinates and the synthetic rate for measured participation;
the population join and maps are unchanged.

## Lessons Learned

**Key takeaways and recommendations:**

- **People-weighting matters**: averaging travel time per area over-counts large
  rural authorities. Weighting by population reproduces the people-based
  headline ("most within 12 minutes") that an unweighted map would miss.
- **Distance is a first-order proxy, routing is the refinement**: straight-line
  distance gets the pattern and the access statistic right cheaply; a routing
  engine is only needed when the literal drive-time figure is the deliverable.
- **Maps turn coverage into targets**: ranking authorities by travel time points
  directly at where a new collection point cuts the longest trips — the evidence
  the campaign needed to lobby local authorities.
- **Composable connectors**: boundaries + population join on `geography_code`
  with no glue code, so the same workflow extends to car ownership, housing type
  or deprivation as further explanatory factors.


## Smart Works Women & Unemployment

# Smart Works Woman Unemployment Analysis

**Reference article:** [DataKind UK - Smart Works](https://www.datakind.org.uk/stories-news/smart-works)

**More about what Smart Works is doing:** [Smart Works](https://www.smartworks.org.uk/)

## Problem Statement

Smart Works needed to identify gaps in their service provision and optimize their outreach strategy to reach more unemployed women who could benefit from their support.

**Key Challenge**: With over 632,500 unemployed women in their operating areas, Smart Works was not reaching all potential beneficiaries and struggled to identify service gaps.

**Key objectives:**

- Map the distribution of Smart Works clients across Local Authorities
- Identify areas with high unemployment but low client numbers
- Analyze demographic disparities between clients and national unemployment data
- Optimize outreach strategy and inform future center locations

**Research Questions:**

- Which Local Authorities have high unemployment rates but low Smart Works client numbers?
- Are there specific demographic groups (age, ethnicity) that Smart Works is under-serving?
- Where should Smart Works focus their efforts or consider opening new centers?
- How do Smart Works client demographics compare to national unemployment patterns?

## Dataset Involved

**Primary Data Sources**:

- **Census 2021**: Comprehensive demographic and employment data by Local Authority
- **Annual Population Survey**: Current unemployment statistics and trends
- **Smart Works Internal Data**: Client records with geographic and demographic information

**Data Integration**: Publicly available 'open data' from Census 2021 and Annual Population Survey was mapped to show women's unemployment rates by Local Authority and compared to Smart Works client distribution.

**Analysis Scope**:

- Geographic comparison of unemployment rates vs. client numbers
- Demographic analysis comparing Smart Works clients to overall unemployed women population

## Desired Output

![Smart Works map](../images/case-studies/smart-works-map.jpg)
*Figure 1: Geographic distribution of Smart Works clients compared to unemployment rates across Local Authorities*

**Key Findings:**

- **Service Gaps Identified**: Several Local Authorities with high unemployment rates showed low numbers of existing Smart Works clients
- **Demographic Disparity**: High unemployment among young women, who appear to be under-served by Smart Works
- **Strategic Opportunities**: Clear geographic areas where Smart Works could expand their reach
- **Outreach Optimization**: Evidence-based guidance for future center locations and targeted outreach

## Replicating the Output with KindTech

### Data Requirements

**Internal Dataset**: Smart Works client records with:

- Geographic location (Local Authority)
- Demographic information (age, ethnicity)
- Service usage patterns

**External Datasets**:

- **Census 2021**: Local Authority-level unemployment and demographic data
- **Annual Population Survey**: Current unemployment statistics
- **Local Authority Boundaries**: Geographic polygons for spatial analysis and mapping

### Analysis Workflow

1. **Data Collection**: Gather Smart Works center locations and client data by geography
2. **Data Integration**: Join internal data with census unemployment data by Local Authority
3. **Spatial Analysis**: Overlay client distribution with LAD boundary data to create UK-wide map
4. **Demographic Comparison**: Compare Smart Works client demographics to overall unemployed women population
5. **Gap Analysis**: Identify areas with high need but low service provision

### Reproduction

A runnable, end-to-end reproduction lives in
[`examples/smart_works_unemployment.py`](https://github.com/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/smart_works_unemployment.py)
(a [marimo](https://marimo.io/) notebook). It uses only the public KindTech
API plus a deterministic synthetic client list (the real client records are
private):

[![Open in marimo](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/smart_works_unemployment.py)
&nbsp;— run it live in the browser (the molab cloud runtime fetches real ONS
data), or locally with `uv run marimo edit examples/smart_works_unemployment.py`.

```python
from uk_open_data import geodata_to_properties, load_geodata, load_ons

# Female, unemployed, by age band, all LADs — Census 2021 table RM024
unemp = load_ons(
    "NM_2124_1",
    geography_type="LAD",
    time="latest",
    c2021_eastat_7=2,  # Unemployed
    c_sex=1,           # Female
    c2021_age_7=[2, 3, 4, 5],  # 16-24, 25-34, 35-49, 50-64
)

# LAD boundaries with centroids, normalised to share `geography_code`
geojson = load_geodata(geography_type="LAD", year="2025", boundary_type="BUC")
```

!!! note "Why Census 2021, not the Annual Population Survey?"
    APS unemployment *counts* by sex are suppressed for small samples — only
    ~40 of 350 Local Authorities return data, and age bands are sparser still.
    Census 2021 (table RM024, `NM_2124_1`) covers **every** LAD in England &
    Wales (318 areas, ~580,000 unemployed women), making it the reliable
    source for a choropleth.

Synthetic client numbers are modelled so reach **decays with distance** from
Smart Works' real centre cities (Birmingham, Manchester, Leeds, Newcastle,
Reading, Bristol, London, etc.), scaled by local female unemployment. This
deliberately reproduces the case study's structure: high-need areas far from
any centre end up under-served.

**Geographic gap** — female unemployment (the need) vs Smart Works reach
(clients per 100 unemployed women). Areas that are dark on the left but pale
on the right are the service gaps:

![Reproduced Smart Works maps](../images/case-studies/smart-works-reproduced-maps.png)
*Figure 2: Female unemployment by Local Authority (left) vs synthetic Smart
Works reach (right). The most under-served high-need areas — Cornwall,
Plymouth, the rural east, and coastal towns — sit far from any centre.*

**Demographic gap** — the age profile of unemployment (need) vs the age
profile of clients reached:

![Reproduced age comparison](../images/case-studies/smart-works-reproduced-age.png)
*Figure 3: The 16-24 band is ~22% of need but only ~12% of clients reached,
flagging young women as under-served — matching the original finding.*

To go from synthetic to real client data, swap `clients_total` for a
`postcode → LAD` aggregation of the real client list. The Census join, the
gap metric, and the maps stay identical.

## Lessons Learned

- **The right source matters more than the obvious one.** The original brief
  named the Annual Population Survey, but APS small-area suppression makes it
  unusable for a full LAD map — Census 2021 is the correct primary source.
- **Distance-decayed reach reproduces the real pattern.** Modelling client
  reach as a function of distance to the nearest centre surfaces exactly the
  high-need, low-provision areas the charity cared about.
- **Normalisation removes the busywork.** Because `load_ons` and
  `load_geodata` both expose `geography_code`, joining statistics to
  boundaries is a single `merge` — no manual column matching.
- **Per-need normalisation reveals gaps counts hide.** "Clients per 100
  unemployed women" exposes under-served areas that a raw client count would
  mask behind population size.


## SOBUS BAME referral mapping

# Sobus BAME hospitalisation analysis

**Reference article:** [DataKind UK - Sobus](https://www.datakind.org.uk/stories-news/sobus)

**More about what Sobus is doing:** [Sobus](https://sobus.org.uk/)

## Problem Statement

Sobus identified ongoing concerns about the disproportionate numbers of BAME (Black, Asian, and Minority Ethnic) people diagnosed with mental health conditions and under the care of mental health services, coupled with inadequate service provision to these communities.

**Key Challenge**: There was a lack of comprehensive local data mapping the BAME mental health landscape, making it difficult to understand the scope and nature of service gaps.

**Research Questions**:

- Was there a disproportionate representation of BAME people diagnosed and under the care of Mental Health Services?
- What was the current service provision for the BAME community suffering from mental health issues?
- How could data-driven insights inform more equitable mental health service delivery?

**Objective**: To map the BAME mental health landscape locally as a starting point for addressing service disparities and improving access to appropriate mental health support.

## Dataset Involved

The project successfully obtained data from multiple sources to provide a comprehensive view of mental health services in West London:

- **West London NHS Trust**: Main provider of mental health services across three boroughs (Hammersmith & Fulham, Ealing, and Hounslow)
- **Hammersmith & Fulham GP Federation**: Primary care data to understand community-level health patterns
- **LBH&F Social Care Data**: Local authority social care information
- **Sobus Sector Survey**: Primary research to capture community perspectives and service gaps

## Desired Output

![Referrals by region](../images/case-studies/distribution-of-clients.jpg)
*Figure 1: Distribution of mental health referrals by region in Hammersmith and Fulham*

**Key Findings**:

- **Disproportionate Representation**: BAME communities were overrepresented in mental health care, with rates 3-8 times higher than white equivalents across various diagnoses
- **Service Quality Gap**: The quality of health service support in the region was below the London average
- **Critical Self-Harm Rates**: Hammersmith & Fulham recorded the highest rate of BAME self-harm incidents in London

## Replicating the Output with KindTech

### Data Requirements

**Internal Dataset**: West London NHS Trust anonymised referral data broken down by ethnicity for Hammersmith and Fulham, with outcode (postcode prefix) attached to each referral for geographic analysis.

### Analysis Workflow

1. **Geographic Mapping**: Convert outcodes to LSOA (Lower Layer Super Output Area) codes
2. **Per-Capita Calculation**: Compute the number of referrals per capita for each LSOA
3. **Visualization**: Create geographic maps showing referral density and ethnic distribution patterns

### Reproduction

A runnable, end-to-end reproduction lives in
[`examples/sobus_bame_referrals.py`](https://github.com/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/sobus_bame_referrals.py)
(a [marimo](https://marimo.io/) notebook). It chains three KindTech connectors,
all joining on the 2021 LSOA `geography_code`:

[![Open in marimo](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/sobus_bame_referrals.py)
&nbsp;— run it live in the browser (the molab cloud runtime fetches real ONS
data), or locally with `uv run marimo edit examples/sobus_bame_referrals.py`.

```python
from uk_open_data import outcode_to_geography, load_ons, load_geodata

# 1. A referral's outcode -> LSOA (the step real referral data would use)
outcode_to_geography(["W6", "W12", "W14"], geography_type="LSOA")

# 2. Ethnic composition per LSOA (Census 2021 TS021), restricted to the borough
eth = load_ons(
    "NM_2041_1",
    geography="1778385172TYPE151",  # LSOAs within Hammersmith & Fulham
    time="latest",
    c2021_eth_20=[0, 1004],  # Total, White -> BAME = Total - White
)
```

!!! note "Everything is on 2021 LSOAs — no crosswalk"
    The postcode connector returns 2021 LSOA codes, **Census 2021** is on 2021
    LSOAs (and gives the population denominator *and* the BAME share), and the
    default LSOA boundaries are 2021. So ethnicity, population and referral
    geography line up on one `geography_code` with no vintage conversion.

!!! warning "Outcode → LSOA is a rough, centroid-based stand-in"
    An outcode (e.g. `W6`) spans many LSOAs, so `outcode_to_geography` returns
    only the LSOA at its centroid — and a centroid can even fall in a
    neighbouring borough. With **full** postcodes use `postcodes_to_geography`
    for an exact mapping. The analysis below runs at true LSOA resolution from
    the census; the outcode step only demonstrates the mechanism.

Real NHS Trust referrals are confidential, so the notebook generates synthetic
referrals per LSOA at a rate that **rises with the area's BAME share**, and
models a BAME resident as more likely to be referred than a White resident —
reproducing the over-representation the study tested for.

**Where is the need?** — BAME share of population (left) and synthetic referral
rate (right). Shared dark areas mean referrals come from the most-BAME LSOAs:

![Reproduced Sobus maps](../images/case-studies/sobus-reproduced-maps.png)
*Figure 2: BAME share of population (left) vs synthetic mental-health referrals
per 1,000 residents (right) across Hammersmith & Fulham's 115 LSOAs. The
hotspots align.*

**Are BAME residents over-represented?** Each LSOA's BAME share against its
referral rate:

![Reproduced Sobus scatter](../images/case-studies/sobus-reproduced-scatter.png)
*Figure 3: A clear positive correlation between BAME share and referrals per
capita — the direction the original study found. Across the borough BAME
residents are ~37% of the population but a higher share of referrals.*

To run on real data, feed each referral's postcode through
`postcodes_to_geography(..., "LSOA")`, tag it with the patient's ethnicity, and
aggregate per `geography_code`; the census join, per-capita maths and maps are
unchanged.

## Lessons Learned

**Key takeaways and recommendations:**

- **Geography reveals disparity**: mapping referrals against ethnic composition
  at LSOA level exposes where need concentrates and quantifies
  over-representation — the starting point Sobus wanted for addressing service
  gaps.
- **Per-capita normalisation matters**: raw referral counts track population
  size; normalising by residents reveals true demand independent of how many
  people live in each area.
- **Postcode resolution drives accuracy**: full postcodes map cleanly to LSOAs;
  outcodes only approximate via a centroid and can cross borough boundaries, so
  the granularity of the source postcode caps the analysis.
- **Census is the denominator**: 2021 ethnic-group data on 2021 LSOAs joins
  natively to referral geography, no crosswalk needed.


## Starlight Children's Foundation

# Starlight mapping children's needs

**Reference article:** [DataKind UK - Starlight](https://www.datakind.org.uk/stories-news/starlight)

**More about what Starlight is doing:** [Starlight](https://www.starlight.org.uk/)

## Problem Statement

Starlight Children's Foundation needed to understand where there is overlap between their services, hospital play provision, and donors to make strategic decisions about service provision and fundraising efforts.

**Key objectives:**

- Map the distribution of Starlight services across the UK
- Identify gaps in play provision and service coverage
- Analyze disparities between different ethnicities and demographics
- Optimize resource allocation based on demonstrated need

**Research Questions:**

- Where are the gaps between Starlight's services and areas of greatest need?
- How does play provision vary across different regions and demographics?
- What factors influence the distribution of hospital play services?
- How can Starlight be more strategic in directing resources to areas with the greatest need?

## Dataset Involved

**Primary Data Collection**: Much of the data had to be collected through freedom of information (FOI) requests from 140 hospital trusts and health boards across the UK.

**Data Types Collected:**

- Number of child admissions by hospital
- Level of play provision and specialist staff
- Play budgets and resource allocation
- Geographic location of services

**Response Rate**: 87% of trusts responded, with some gaps in the data for those that did respond, suggesting that potentially useful data is not being systematically collected.

**Geospatial Processing**: Geographic data was processed and standardized to enable efficient map visualizations and spatial analysis.

## Desired Output

![Starlight map](../images/case-studies/starlight-signed-up-centres.jpg)
*Figure 1: Starlight heat map showing distribution of signed-up centres across the UK*

**Key Findings:**

- **Even Resource Distribution**: Starlight's resources were spread evenly over deprived and less deprived areas, indicating potential for more targeted allocation
- **Service Gaps Identified**: Some regions had more eligible trusts than were receiving play provisions
- **Admission vs. Service Mismatch**: Other regions had significantly more hospital admissions than boxes distributed
- **Strategic Opportunity**: Clear evidence that Starlight could be more strategic about directing help to places with the greatest need

## Replicating the Output with KindTech

### Data Requirements

**Synthetic Data Generation**: Create realistic datasets representing:

- Play provision levels across clinical commissioning groups (CCGs)
- Hospital admission rates for children
- Geographic distribution of Starlight services
- Demographic and deprivation indicators

**Geographic Boundaries**: Clinical commissioning group (CCG) boundaries for spatial analysis and mapping

### Analysis Workflow

1. **Data Generation**: Create synthetic play provision data across clinical regions
2. **Geographic Mapping**: Map data to relevant CCG boundaries for visualization
3. **Gap Analysis**: Identify areas with high need but low service provision
4. **Visualization**: Create heat maps showing service distribution and need indicators

### Reproduction

A runnable, end-to-end reproduction lives in
[`examples/starlight_play_provision.py`](https://github.com/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/starlight_play_provision.py)
(a [marimo](https://marimo.io/) notebook). It maps synthetic provision against
need over England's real NHS commissioning geography:

[![Open in marimo](https://marimo.io/molab-shield.svg)](https://molab.marimo.io/github/KindTechUK/uk-open-data/blob/main/examples/starlight_play_provision.py)
&nbsp;— run it live in the browser (the molab cloud runtime fetches real ONS
data), or locally with `uv run marimo edit examples/starlight_play_provision.py`.

```python
from uk_open_data import load_geodata, geodata_to_properties
import pandas as pd

# England's 42 Integrated Care Boards (the geography that replaced CCGs)
geojson = load_geodata(geography_type="ICB", year="2023", coverage="EN", boundary_type="BSC")
icbs = pd.DataFrame(geodata_to_properties(geojson, "ICB", 2023))
```

!!! note "ICBs, not CCGs"
    Clinical Commissioning Groups were abolished in July 2022 and replaced by
    **Integrated Care Boards**. KindTech serves the current ICB boundaries, so
    the reproduction uses the 42 ICBs as the commissioning unit; the workflow is
    identical to the original CCG analysis.

The original study's admission and provision figures came from FOI returns that
aren't public, so the notebook generates a deterministic stand-in (`rng(3)`)
where **child admissions vary widely** (the need) but **boxes are distributed
roughly evenly** (the resource) — the exact pattern the study flagged.

**Need vs provision** — child admissions (left) and boxes distributed (right).
The two maps *don't* share their dark areas, which is the point:

![Reproduced Starlight maps](../images/case-studies/starlight-reproduced-maps.png)
*Figure 2: Child admissions (left, the need) vs Starlight boxes distributed
(right, the resource) across England's 42 ICBs. Provision does not follow need.*

**Does provision follow need?** Each ICB's admissions against its boxes:

![Reproduced Starlight scatter](../images/case-studies/starlight-reproduced-scatter.png)
*Figure 3: A near-flat (slightly negative) relationship between need and
provision — resources are spread evenly regardless of demand, the
"be more strategic" opportunity the original study identified.*

To run on real data, replace the synthetic columns with Starlight's FOI returns
keyed by ICB (or by trust, then mapped to ICB); the boundary join, coverage
maths and maps are unchanged.

## Lessons Learned

**Key takeaways and recommendations:**

- **Map provision against need, not in isolation**: plotting boxes alongside
  admissions on the same geography immediately exposes the decoupling that a
  provision-only view hides.
- **Even distribution is a finding, not a default**: a near-flat
  need-vs-provision relationship is itself the evidence that allocation could
  be more strategic.
- **Coverage ratios rank the opportunity**: boxes per 1,000 admissions turns
  the gap into an ordered list of where redirecting resource helps most.
- **Stable geography matters**: serving current ICB boundaries (post-CCG) keeps
  the analysis aligned with how the NHS commissions today, with no manual
  crosswalk.


# User Guide

## Overview

# API Reference

KindTech provides four modules for accessing UK public data, and analyses that
put them to work on your own data:

## Modules

### [Geographic Data](geo.md) — `uk_open_data.geo`

Load UK geographic boundary data from the ONS ArcGIS Geoportal. Returns GeoJSON.

```python
from uk_open_data.geo import load_geodata

# Load Local Authority Districts
boundaries = load_geodata(geography_type="LAD", coverage="UK")
```

### [ONS Statistics](ons.md) — `uk_open_data.ons`

Load statistical data from the ONS NOMIS API. Returns pandas or polars DataFrames.

```python
from uk_open_data.ons import load_ons

# Load Jobseeker's Allowance data
df = load_ons("NM_1_1", geography="TYPE480", time="latest")
```

### [Postcodes](postcodes.md) — `uk_open_data.postcodes`

Resolve UK postcodes (and outcodes) to ONS geography codes via postcodes.io, so
address data joins to boundaries and statistics. Returns pandas or polars
DataFrames.

```python
from uk_open_data.postcodes import postcodes_to_geography

# Postcodes -> LSOA, ready to join on `geography_code`
located = postcodes_to_geography(["SE13 7HX", "SE6 4RU"], geography_type="LSOA")
```

### [Deprivation (IMD)](imd.md) — `uk_open_data.imd`

Load UK Indices of Multiple Deprivation, keyed on geography codes. A single
nation returns its **official** index (England IoD 2025/2019 with all domains,
or WIMD/SIMD/NIMDM); `nation="UK"` returns the mySociety composite for
cross-nation comparison. Returns pandas or polars DataFrames.

```python
from uk_open_data.imd import load_imd

imd = load_imd(nation="England")  # official IoD 2025; join on `geography_code`
```

### [Analyses](analyses.md) — `uk_open_data.analyses`

Ask a question of your own data. An analysis joins your table to open data and
returns figures with their sources, the working, the choices made and the
checks a person should do. Results hold totals only, never rows.

```python
from uk_open_data.analyses import run_analysis

result = run_analysis(
    "reach-deprivation", clients, columns={"postcode": "Client postcode"}
)
```

## Design principles

- **Flat functions** — no classes to instantiate, just call `load_geodata()` or `load_ons()`
- **String or enum** — pass `"LAD"` or `GeographyType.LAD`, both work
- **Bring your own DataFrame** — narwhals returns whatever backend you have installed
- **Bundled catalogs** — small CSV reference tables ship with the package (136KB total) so you can browse available datasets offline
- **Live data** — actual geographic/statistical data is always fetched fresh from the source APIs


## Analyses

# Analyses

An analysis answers one question a charity asks of its own data. You give it a
table, say which column is which, and it joins your data to UK open data and
returns figures you can check and reuse.

Kindtech Evidence is built on these analyses. This page is about running them
from Python. You can also run them from the [command line](cli.md), or from a
chat assistant through the [connector](connector.md).

These analyses follow work first done by
[DataKind UK](https://www.datakind.org.uk/) volunteers with charities. The
[case studies](../case-studies/index.md) reproduce five of those projects.

Every analysis returns the same things:

- **an answer**: one or two sentences that answer the question, and the
  three figures to show first
- **figures**: the headline numbers
- **tables**: totals behind the figures
- **a map description**: which areas to draw and what to colour them by, when
  the analysis has a map
- **chart descriptions**: which table and columns to draw as a bar chart
- **the working**: each step taken, with how many rows went in and came out,
  the figures before rounding and the code that runs it again
- **choices**: what the analysis decided for you, and the option that changes it
- **checks**: what a person must confirm before using the figures
- **caveats**: what the figures cannot say
- **sources**: publisher, edition, licence and link for every dataset used
- **a privacy summary**: what was hidden, and what left your machine

A result holds totals only. Nothing in it describes one person, and no value
from your data is repeated back, not even in a warning or an error message.

## Quick start

```python
import pandas as pd
from uk_open_data.analyses import run_analysis

clients = pd.read_csv("clients.csv")

result = run_analysis(
    "reach-deprivation",
    clients,
    columns={"postcode": "Client postcode"},
)

result.answer                                   # the question, answered in a sentence
result.figure("share_most_deprived_20").value   # 41.3 (per cent)
result.table("by_decile").to_frame()            # pandas or polars DataFrame
[check.question for check in result.checks]     # what to confirm first
result.to_dict()                                # everything, as plain JSON types
```

`data` can be a pandas or polars DataFrame, or a list of row dictionaries.
`columns` maps each role the analysis needs to one of your column names. You can
leave a role out when your data already has a column with that name.

To run an analysis on a file without writing Python, use the
[command line](cli.md).

## Functions

### `list_analyses()`

Returns an `AnalysisInfo` for every analysis: its `id`, `title`, the `question` it
answers, a `summary`, its `roles` (the columns it can use), its `input_modes`
(the shapes of data it accepts), its `options` and its `coverage`.

Every option has two names. `name` is its code name, the one a call is
written with, such as `catchment`. `label` is its short plain name, such as
"Area you serve". Show the label beside the option. Every message that points a
person at an option uses the label, in quotes ("Change 'Area you serve' to
include them."), and never the code name, so the sentence matches what is on
the screen. An option has the same label in every analysis that has it, and
the result's `choices` use the same label for the choice it made:

| `name` | `label` |
| --- | --- |
| `catchment` | Area you serve |
| `catchment_min_share` | Share that makes a place part of your area |
| `suppress_below` | Smallest count shown |
| `postcode_lookup` | Where postcodes are looked up |
| `need` | People you are trying to reach |
| `top` | Places listed |
| `characteristic` | What people are grouped by |
| `groups` | How your labels match census groups |
| `under_represented_below` | What counts as under-represented |
| `within_km` | Distance within reach, in kilometres |

The area an analysis looks across has one name wherever a person reads it:
"the area you serve". `catchment` is only its code name.

A table's columns have plain names too. `table.columns` holds the ids, which a
program reads, and `table.headings` maps each id to the heading to show, such
as "Your people per 100 in need" for `people_per_100_in_need`. `table.units`
gives the unit of each column that has one, named as the units of figures
are: `"percent"` or `"km"`. Show a table with its headings and units and it
reads the same on a page, in a chat and on the command line. A place is a
"Local authority" in most tables and a "Neighbourhood" in the one behind the
first analysis's map.

An option that takes one of a fixed list of values lists them as `choices`,
each with a `value` and a `label` a person can read, so a page can show a list
to pick from. `choices` is empty when the option is free, such as a number or
a place name. For the `need` option the choices are the built-in needs; a table
of your own is still given as a mapping.

A role with `reported` set to `True` holds names the result uses too, such as
local authorities, so the same names can appear in the result. Values of every
other role are never repeated.

A reported role can also list `reported_values`. That is for a column that
holds a person's own words as well, such as their ethnic group: only the
listed values are names the result uses, and no other value in the column is
ever repeated. If you check a result for values repeated from the input, leave
out the listed values when there are any, compared without case, and check
every other value in the column. Leave the whole column out only when the
role is reported and lists no values.

A role with `amount` set to `True` holds a number the analysis adds up: a count of
people or a volume. A total of it is in the result, so where one row is the
only one for its place or group, that row's number comes back as the total.
That is not a repeated value. A number in any other role, such as a latitude,
never comes back.

### `describe_analysis(analysis_id)`

Returns the `AnalysisInfo` for one analysis. Raises `KeyError` for an unknown id.

### `run_analysis(analysis_id, data, columns=None, options=None)`

Runs an analysis and returns an `AnalysisResult`.

Raises `AnalysisInputError` (a `ValueError`) when the data, the column mapping or
an option cannot be used. The message is written for a person and
`error.problems` lists each problem separately.

`error.option` is the code name of the option the error is about, and
`error.role` the name of the column role, so a page can mark the right box and
a program need not search the sentence. When the problems are about several,
it is the first of them. Each is `None` when the error is about neither, for
example when a source could not be read. The command line adds what to type:
"On the command line this is --option catchment=VALUE."

When the columns an analysis needs were not all found, `error.role` is the
first one still to be named. When an option was given that the analysis does
not have, the message lists each option it does have by both names:
"need ('People you are trying to reach')".

When a public data source the analysis needs cannot be reached, the
`requests.RequestException` is let out. Its text holds the whole web address
that was asked for, which can hold a postcode, so show a message of your own
rather than the text. The command line names the site alone, and says
whether the source could not be reached or answered with an error. An analysis
needs no network when the public figures it uses are kept on your machine.

### `record_run(analysis_id, input_mode, door)`

Records that a run has given a person an answer, so that a host can count how
often each analysis is used. It writes one record at `INFO` level to the
`uk_open_data.runs` logger, and that is all it does: the package adds no handler
and sends nothing anywhere. On a person's own machine nobody collects the
records. A host that keeps its logs can count them.

```python
from uk_open_data.analyses import record_run

record_run(result.analysis_id, result.input_mode, "page")
# run analysis=reach-deprivation mode=postcodes door=page
```

`run_analysis` never records a run by itself. Whatever gives the answer to a
person calls `record_run` once, after the answer has been given: the command
line does (`"cli"`), and a page (`"page"`) or a chat assistant (`"chat"`) built
on these analyses should. A run that fails is not recorded.

The record holds the three words and nothing else. Each must be on a fixed
list (a registered analysis, one of its input modes, one of the three doors),
so no word from a person's data can reach a log. A word that is not on its list
raises `KeyError` (the analysis) or `ValueError` (the mode or the door), and the
message does not repeat it. The same three words are on the record as
`record.analysis_id`, `record.input_mode` and `record.door`.

A host that keeps the records imports the logger's name, and the doors, from
the package, so neither is typed out a second time:

```python
import logging

from uk_open_data.analyses import DOORS, RUNS_LOGGER

logging.getLogger(RUNS_LOGGER).setLevel(logging.INFO)
```

## Drawing the map

A result describes its map; `render_map` draws it as an SVG picture with a
key and the credits the data licences ask for.

```python
from uk_open_data.analyses import render_map

svg = render_map(result)                  # the first layer: deprivation decile
svg = render_map(result, layer="people")  # people reached, in bands

with open("map.svg", "w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    handle.write(svg)
```

The picture is drawn from the result's own table of totals, so it shows
nothing the result does not already hold. People are shown in bands, and the
lowest band includes zero. Hover over an area in a browser to see its name and
value. The colours adapt to a dark page.

A picture shows one layer, and its title says what the colour shows: "People
reached, by neighbourhood". The first layer of a map is drawn in blue and the
second in orange, so two pictures of one result do not look like the same
measure. The shaded areas sit in a frame with a scale line. Up to twelve
local authorities are named one by one; neighbourhoods are named by the local
authority they are in. A name that would cover most of a small place is
written beside it, where there is room, so its colour can be seen. Text is broken into lines to fit the width you ask for.

The places around the map are drawn in pale grey, with their names where a
name fits, when you give their outlines. Only the part of each that the frame
shows is written to the picture, so a large neighbour does not make the file
large. Put them among the features of
`boundaries`, or in a list under `"surroundings"`. Codes listed under
`"focus"` are the surrounding places that hold the shaded areas: each gets a
darker line and its name. Codes listed under `"shore"` are surrounding places
whose outline is where the land ends. The shaded areas are drawn no further
than it, and the picture is framed on it. Use it when the outlines of the
areas run out over water and the outline of the place that holds them does
not.

```python
boundaries = {
    "type": "FeatureCollection",
    "features": areas,           # outlines you already have
    "surroundings": nearby,
    "focus": ["E09000023"],
    "shore": ["E09000023"],
}
svg = render_map(result, boundaries=boundaries)
```

`render_map` fetches the outline of each area from the ONS Open Geography
Portal. Only the public area codes of the area you serve, and of the local
authorities near it, are sent. To draw without the network, pass `boundaries=`
a GeoJSON FeatureCollection you already have; `load_map_boundaries(result)`
fetches one you can save and reuse.

`load_map_boundaries` fetches the places around the map as well, and lists
under `"focus"` the local authorities that hold a map's neighbourhoods. A map
of up to 1,000 neighbourhoods or 20 local authorities is drawn large, so its
outlines come from the full ones with detail finer than 10 or 20 metres left
out. So do the local authorities that hold its neighbourhoods, and the other
places a picture of the usual width shows when there are no more than 40 of
them, so that neighbours meet. A place further off keeps its 200 metre
outline.

The full outlines of local authorities stop at the shore. The only full
outlines of neighbourhoods that are open run out to low water and to the
middle of a river. So on a map of neighbourhoods the local authorities that
hold them are also listed under `"shore"`, and a river or a bay is left
clear. When the fine outline of one of them does not come, nothing is listed
and the neighbourhoods are drawn whole.

A map of more areas is drawn small and takes outlines simplified to 200
metres. Every map asks for every local authority at 200 metres, nearly three
megabytes, to find the ones near it. That answer is kept in memory for the
life of the process, so a second map does not ask again;
`uk_open_data.analyses.maps.clear_outline_cache()` forgets it. When the places around cannot be fetched, the map is drawn without
them and nothing is said.

The fine outlines usually come in a few seconds. At times the service has
taken from a quarter of a minute to a minute or two for one map, and it is
not known why. A program that cannot wait,
such as one answering in a chat, calls `load_map_boundaries(result,
fine=False)`. It then gets the 200 metre outlines of every area, and the
places around from the answer kept in memory, in a second or two.
`load_map_boundaries` is safe to call from two threads at once.

## The answer

`result.answer` is one or two sentences that answer the question the analysis
asks, for example:

> Of your people in the area you serve, 49.0% live in the 20% most deprived
> neighbourhoods in England. Of everyone who lives in that area, 20.0% do, so
> you reach those neighbourhoods more than their share.

Open with it wherever you show a result, so a report, a page and a chat
assistant all say the same thing. It is built from the figures and tables of
the result, after small counts are hidden, so it says nothing the result does
not already show. When the figure it rests on is hidden, it says so instead of
giving a number. The places and groups it names are the public names in the
result's tables, never text from your data.

The sentence is careful about what it calls a gap. A place is named as one to
look at first only when it falls below the rate for the whole area, so a list
of one or two places does not present the place you reach most as a gap, and a
place whose count is hidden is not named. A count of every resident is called
"residents", not "people in need". A group with nobody in your data is named
last, with a line saying so, because it may be a group you do not record.

`result.key_figures` holds the ids of up to three figures to show first, in
order. Each is a figure of the result, and none is hidden: when a figure that
would be shown first is hidden to protect a small count, the next one takes
its place.

```python
for figure_id in result.key_figures:
    figure = result.figure(figure_id)
    print(figure.label, figure.value, figure.unit)
```

## Checking a result and running it again

A result shows its working, so that anyone can check it or run it again.

`result.working` lists each step in plain words, with how many rows went in
and came out. `result.sources` gives each source and its date.

A share or a rate is rounded before it is shown. `figure.exact` is the value
before rounding:

```python
figure = result.figure("share_most_deprived_20")
figure.value   # 68.6
figure.exact   # 68.57142857142857
```

`exact` is `None` for a count, which is not rounded, and for a figure that is
hidden to protect a small count. It is also `None` for a distance from one
place to a site, which is rounded to the kilometre on purpose so that it says
less about where a site is.

`result.code` is the Python that runs the analysis again with the same
settings:

```python
print(result.code)
```

```python
# Version 0.1 of this analysis, run with
# uk-open-data 0.2.0. This runs it again with
# the same settings. No row or heading of your table is written
# here: put the name of your own column beside each role.
import pandas as pd

from uk_open_data.analyses import run_analysis

data = pd.read_csv("your-table.csv")
result = run_analysis(
    "reach-deprivation",
    data,
    columns={
        "postcode": "",  # the name of your column
    },
    options={
        "suppress_below": 10,
        "postcode_lookup": "auto",
        "catchment_min_share": 0.05,
    },
)
print(result.answer)
for figure in result.figures:
    print(figure.label, figure.value)
```

It prints the answer and every figure, to set beside the ones in the result.

Every setting that has a value is written out, the ones you left alone too,
so the code gives the same result if a default changes in a later version.
That is why it can hold a setting the list of choices in a result does not
mention. A setting the analysis works out for itself, such as the area you
serve when you named none, is left out. An area you named is written as you
gave it.

The setting for where postcodes are looked up is written as it was used. Code
copied from a run that kept postcodes on one machine says so, and on another
machine it stops and asks for the postcode table before it sends a postcode
anywhere.

The code holds no row and no heading of your table. The names of your columns
are left for you to fill in, because a heading can hold something private. A
setting that holds your own words, such as your own labels for groups in
`who-we-miss`, is written as `{}` with a note to fill it in. So the code is as
safe to share as the result is.

The command line prints both as the last two parts of its report, under
"Figures before rounding" and "To run it again in Python". The code starts at
the margin, so it runs as it is copied.

## Charts

`result.charts` describes the charts a result is best shown with, so a page
can draw them without knowing the analysis. Each `Chart` names a table of the
result, the column that names each group of bars (`category_column`) and one
or more `series`, each a column with a label and a unit. Every series in a
chart has the same unit, so one axis serves them all.

```python
chart = result.charts[0]
frame = result.table(chart.table).to_frame()
frame.plot.bar(x=chart.category_column, y=[s.column for s in chart.series])
```

A value hidden to protect a small count is `None` in the table. Draw no bar
for it.

## Small counts

A count from 1 to 4 that is about a named place or a group is returned as
`None`, with `suppressed` set to `True`, and so is anything worked out from it.
When hiding one cell would let it be worked out from a total, a second cell is
hidden with it. So a hidden count is not always small: do not report a hidden
cell as "fewer than 5". Every result says this in its privacy notes. Change
the threshold with the `suppress_below` option; it cannot go below 3.

A result says which threshold was used in `privacy.suppress_below`. The analyses
about sites, provision gap and access and distance, hide nothing, and for them
it is `None`.

## Reach against deprivation

`reach-deprivation` answers: are we reaching people in the most deprived
neighbourhoods? It covers England, using the English Indices of Deprivation
2025 on 2021 neighbourhoods (LSOAs).

It accepts two shapes of data:

| Input mode | Columns | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `postcodes` | `postcode` | One row per person or case, with a home postcode |
| `neighbourhood_counts` | `lsoa_code`, `count` | Already totalled by 2021 LSOA |

In `postcodes` mode the analysis looks postcodes up in the
[postcode table on your machine](postcodes.md#looking-up-postcodes-on-this-machine)
when one is installed, and then no postcode is sent anywhere. Install it once
with `uk-open-data postcodes download`. Without the table, the distinct,
well-formed postcodes are sent to [postcodes.io](https://postcodes.io/); no
other column leaves your machine, and rows that are blank or not shaped like a
postcode are never sent. The result says which happened, under `choices` and
`privacy`. In `neighbourhood_counts` mode nothing leaves your machine.

The deprivation index is downloaded from gov.uk, or read from a copy
[kept on your machine](imd.md#keeping-the-english-index-on-this-machine) when
there is one. A result that used a copy says so in its `sources` and its
`working`, with the note the copy was kept with.

The analysis then works out **the area you serve**: the local authorities that each
hold at least 5% of the people it could place. The decile figures and the map
are about the people who live there, so they can be set against everyone who
lives there. People outside the area you serve are counted in the local authority
table, and a warning says how many there are.

| Figure | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `people_supplied` | People in the data you gave |
| `people_located` | People placed in an English neighbourhood |
| `people_in_catchment` | People who live in the area you serve |
| `share_most_deprived_10` | Share of them in the 10% most deprived neighbourhoods in England |
| `share_most_deprived_20` | Share of them in the 20% most deprived neighbourhoods in England |
| `catchment_share_most_deprived_20` | Share of residents of the area you serve who live in those neighbourhoods, for comparison |
| `reach_per_1000_most_deprived_20` | People reached per 1,000 residents of those neighbourhoods |
| `reach_per_1000_elsewhere` | People reached per 1,000 residents in the rest of the area you serve |

The chart `people_by_decile` sets the share of your people in each decile
against the share of residents of the area you serve.

| Table | Rows |
| --- | --- |
| `by_decile` | One per deprivation decile: people, share of people, residents, share of residents, people per 1,000 |
| `by_local_authority` | One per local authority; authorities outside the area you serve with few people share one unnamed row |
| `by_neighbourhood` | One per neighbourhood in the area you serve: decile, residents, and people in bands. This feeds the map |

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `suppress_below` | `5` | Counts above zero and below this are hidden |
| `postcode_lookup` | `"auto"` | `"offline"` uses the table on your machine and fails without one, `"online"` uses postcodes.io, `"auto"` uses the table when it is installed |
| `catchment` | worked out | A local authority name or code, a list of them, or `"England"` |
| `catchment_min_share` | `0.05` | The share a local authority needs to join a worked-out area |

```python
result = run_analysis(
    "reach-deprivation",
    clients,
    columns={"postcode": "Client postcode"},
    options={"catchment": ["Lewisham", "Greenwich"]},
)
```

!!! note "Before you use the figures"
    Read `result.checks` and `result.caveats`. Deprivation is measured for
    neighbourhoods, not people: someone who lives in a deprived neighbourhood
    is not necessarily deprived.

## Need against reach

`need-reach` answers: where is need high and our presence low? It covers
England and Wales, by local authority, and is the method of the
[Smart Works case study](../case-studies/smart-works-woman-unemployment.md)
turned into a function.

It accepts two shapes of data:

| Input mode | Columns | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `postcodes` | `postcode` | One row per person or case, with a home postcode |
| `area_counts` | `local_authority`, `count` | Already totalled by local authority, named or coded |

Postcodes are placed as in the first analysis: on your machine when the postcode
table is installed, and with postcodes.io otherwise.

The analysis loads a count of **people in need** in every local authority from
[Nomis](ons.md), divides the people you helped in each one by it, and lists
the high-need local authorities where you reach the fewest people per 100 in
need. A local authority is high need when its count is in the top quarter of
the area you serve. With fewer than four places, the one with the largest count
is high need.

Choose the need with the `need` option:

| `need` | People counted |
| --- | --- |
| `"unemployed"` (default) | Unemployed people aged 16 to 64, not counting full-time students, Census 2021 |
| `"unemployed_women"` | Unemployed women aged 16 to 64, not counting full-time students, Census 2021 |
| `"unemployed_men"` | Unemployed men aged 16 to 64, not counting full-time students, Census 2021 |
| `"residents"` | Everyone who lives there, of every age, Census 2021. Use it when what you offer is for anyone |
| `{"dataset": ..., "label": ..., "filters": {...}}` | Any table Nomis publishes by local authority. The filters are the category codes to add up. Counts are asked for (`measures` 20100) unless the filters name another measure |

The three unemployment needs count the census group "Economically active
(excluding full-time students): Unemployed", as the case study does. Full-time
students who were looking for work are a separate census group and are not
counted. To count them too, give the table form with both groups:

```python
options = {
    "need": {
        "dataset": "NM_2124_1",
        "label": "Unemployed people aged 16 to 64, with full-time students",
        "filters": {
            "c2021_eastat_7": [2, 4],
            "c_sex": 0,
            "c2021_age_7": [2, 3, 4, 5],
        },
    }
}
```

The need figures are public. They are fetched from Nomis once for each need
and then kept in memory for as long as the program runs;
`clear_need_cache()` forgets them. To run with no request to Nomis at all,
keep a copy on the machine, in the same data folder as the
[postcode table](postcodes.md#looking-up-postcodes-on-this-machine):

```python
from uk_open_data.analyses.need_reach import download_need_figures, keep_need_figures

download_need_figures("unemployed")   # fetch once, when a server is built
download_need_figures("residents")    # so the map can shade need by its rate

# or keep figures of your own under a built-in need, for a demonstration
keep_need_figures(
    "unemployed",
    [("E09000023", "Lewisham", 9000), ("E09000011", "Greenwich", 8000)],
    note="invented for a demonstration.",
)
```

A result that used a kept copy says so in its `sources` and its `working`,
with the note the copy was kept with.

The area you serve should hold the places you do not reach yet as well. Name it with `catchment`: a
list of local authorities, or a country. When you leave it out, the analysis
works the area out as the first analysis does: each local authority that holds
at least 5% of the people located (`catchment_min_share`). When none does,
every local authority in England and Wales is compared.

An area worked out this way holds only places you already reach, so it can
show where your reach is low against need but not where you reach nobody. The
result says so in a warning. To see the places you do not reach, name the area.

| Figure | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `people_supplied` | People in the data you gave |
| `people_located` | People placed in a local authority in England or Wales |
| `people_in_catchment` | People who live in the area you serve |
| `areas_compared` | Local authorities compared |
| `people_in_need` | People in need in the area you serve |
| `reach_per_100_in_need` | People you reached per 100 people in need, across the area |
| `high_need_areas` | Local authorities with high need |
| `high_need_areas_without_people` | High-need local authorities where you reached nobody |
| `share_of_people_in_high_need_areas` | Share of your people who live in high-need local authorities |
| `share_of_need_in_high_need_areas` | Share of people in need who live there, for comparison |

The charts `need_in_priority_areas` and `reach_in_priority_areas` show people
in need and people reached per 100 in need for the places in `priority_areas`.

The labels follow the need. When the need is every resident, the figures, the
headings, the list, the working and the source say "residents" and "the local
authorities with the most residents", not "people in need" and "high need".
The fourth and fifth analyses do the same.

The answer says so when the area was worked out from your data: it opens "In
the 7 local authorities where most of your people live". When a fifth or more
of the people in your data could not be placed in the area you serve, it ends
by saying how many are not counted. When some of them could not be placed in
any local authority, which is a name or a postcode to put right, and others
live outside the area, which is not a mistake, it says how many of each.

When only one local authority is compared every share is 100%, so
`key_figures` names the rate and the two counts behind it instead:
`reach_per_100_in_need`, `people_in_catchment` and `people_in_need`.

| Table | Rows |
| --- | --- |
| `priority_areas` | The high-need local authorities, your lowest reach first: people in need, people, people per 100 in need. It is a list in that order and no more: a place on it can have more reach than the area as a whole |
| `by_local_authority` | One per local authority compared, with need and reach in bands, and people in need for each 1,000 residents. This feeds the map |

The map shades need by its rate, people in need for each 1,000 residents, in
five equal groups. With fewer than five places, each is a group of its own,
from the lowest group to the highest, and one place alone is in the middle
group. The three groups of the reach layer work the same way. The note of a
layer says so when its places are fewer than its groups, and says nothing of
it otherwise. A count would
make the largest places darkest whatever their need. The list of high-need places still goes by the count, as
the case study does. The residents are the census count of everyone who lives
in each local authority, loaded beside the need figures.

The map falls back to the count in two cases, and the result says which way
it went in its choices (`map_need`) and in the note of the map's `need` layer.
One is when the need is every resident, so there is no rate to work out. The
other is when the need figures came from a copy kept on the machine and no
copy of the residents is kept beside it: the analysis does not fetch them, so
that a run kept off the network stays off it.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `suppress_below` | `5` | Counts above zero and below this are hidden |
| `postcode_lookup` | `"auto"` | As for the first analysis |
| `need` | `"unemployed"` | The need to compare your reach with |
| `catchment` | worked out | A local authority name or code, a list of them, or `"England"`, `"Wales"` or `"England and Wales"` |
| `catchment_min_share` | `0.05` | The share a local authority needs to join a worked-out area |
| `top` | `10` | How many places to list, from 1 to 50 |

```python
result = run_analysis(
    "need-reach",
    clients,
    columns={"postcode": "Client postcode"},
    options={"need": "unemployed_women"},
)

result.table("priority_areas").to_frame()
```

A local authority with a hidden count is still ranked. It is ranked as if it
had the largest count that would be hidden, which depends on the threshold
alone, so the order of the list gives nothing away.

!!! note "Before you use the figures"
    Read `result.checks` and `result.caveats`. Low reach is not the same as
    unmet need: another organisation may already serve the place. Need is a
    count of people, so large local authorities are more likely to be listed.

## Who we are missing

`who-we-miss` answers: who do we reach less than their share of the people who
live here? It covers England and Wales, and is the method of the
[Sobus case study](../case-studies/sobus-bame-analysis.md) turned into a
function.

It accepts three shapes of data:

| Input mode | Columns | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `postcodes` | `group`, `postcode` | One row per person, with their group and home postcode |
| `group_counts` | `group`, `count` | Already totalled by group |
| `people` | `group` | One row per person, with their group and no location |

The `group` column holds each person's ethnic group, or their sex, in your own
words. The analysis matches each label to a group the 2021 Census publishes,
counts your people by group, and sets each group's share of your people
against its share of the residents of **the area you serve**. A group is
**under-represented** when its share of your people is below four fifths of
its share of residents.

Choose what the column holds with the `characteristic` option:

| `characteristic` | Groups compared | Census table |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"ethnic_group"` (default) | Asian, Black, Mixed, White, Other | TS021 |
| `"sex"` | Female, Male | TS008 |

Labels are matched by their wording. "Black Caribbean" is Black, "White and
Black Caribbean" is Mixed, "Any other ethnic group" is Other, and "Not stated"
matches nothing. People whose label matches nothing are counted, left out of
the shares, and a warning says how many there are. Codes and short forms
cannot be matched by wording, so say where they belong with the `groups`
option:

```python
result = run_analysis(
    "who-we-miss",
    clients,
    columns={"group": "Ethnicity", "postcode": "Client postcode"},
    options={"groups": {"BAF": "Black", "WBR": "White"}},
)

result.table("by_group").to_frame()
```

The result names the census groups. It never repeats one of your own labels.
The `group` role lists the census group names as its `reported_values`,
because a label of yours can be the same as one of them.

With postcodes the analysis works out the area you serve as the first analysis does: the
local authorities that each hold at least 5% of the people it could place.
People who live outside it are left out, because they are set against the
residents of the area you serve. Without postcodes the analysis cannot tell where you
work, so you must name the area with `catchment`.

The residents come from [Nomis](ons.md), for every local authority at once.
They are public, are fetched once for each characteristic and are then kept in
memory; `clear_residents_cache()` forgets them. To run with no request to
Nomis, keep a copy on the machine, as for need figures:

```python
from uk_open_data.analyses.who_we_miss import download_residents, keep_residents

download_residents("ethnic_group")   # fetch once, when a server is built

# or keep figures of your own, for a demonstration
keep_residents(
    "sex",
    [("E09000023", "Lewisham", {"Female": 156000, "Male": 144000})],
    note="invented for a demonstration.",
)
```

| Figure | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `people_supplied` | People in the data you gave |
| `people_in_catchment` | People set against residents: with postcodes, those who live in the area you serve |
| `people_matched` | People whose label matched a census group. The shares are of these people |
| `people_not_matched` | People with no label, or one that matched no census group |
| `residents` | Residents of the area you serve in the 2021 Census |
| `groups_under_represented` | Groups you reach less than their share of residents |
| `share_of_people_first_group` | Share of your people in the first of those groups |
| `share_of_residents_first_group` | Share of residents in that group |

The last two are the two shares the answer quotes, each with its value before
rounding. They are there when the answer quotes them: when a group is reached
less than its share and has people in your data.

The chart `people_against_residents` sets the share of your people in each
group against the share of residents.

| Table | Rows |
| --- | --- |
| `by_group` | One per census group: people, share of people, residents, share of residents, `representation` (the first share divided by the second) and whether the group is under-represented |

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `suppress_below` | `5` | Counts above zero and below this are hidden |
| `postcode_lookup` | `"auto"` | As for the first analysis |
| `characteristic` | `"ethnic_group"` | What the group column holds |
| `groups` | none | Your label to census group, for labels the wording does not settle |
| `catchment` | worked out from postcodes | A local authority name or code, a list of them, or `"England"`, `"Wales"` or `"England and Wales"`. Needed when there are no postcodes |
| `catchment_min_share` | `0.05` | The share a local authority needs to join a worked-out area |
| `under_represented_below` | `0.8` | A group is under-represented below this fraction of its share of residents |

A group with a hidden count is not judged. A group nobody came from has a
count of zero, which is shown, and is under-represented.

This analysis has no map yet. The residents are compared across the whole
area you serve, not place by place.

!!! note "Before you use the figures"
    Read `result.checks` and `result.caveats`. A gap is not proof of a
    barrier: groups differ in age and in need, and the census counts
    residents of every age. With few people, a gap can be chance. Do not
    publish two runs with different areas side by side, because a small
    count can be worked out by taking one from the other.

## Provision gap
